title: Ang 762–763: the unskilled bride
hookLine: Guru Nanak's poems of the unskilled and the skilled bride
tomorrow: what does a house feel like when the one you waited for walks in?

lines: HOW CAN I GO TO HIM?
cards: The group project where everyone else seems to know what they're doing. The family kitchen where you're the one who can't cook. Feeling clumsy is its own kind of lonely.
Guru Nanak wrote a poem in that voice. On ang 762, Kuchajji, the unskilled bride, begins, in paraphrase: I have no skill, my faults overflow; how can I go to my Husband?

teach.h: KUCHAJJI: WHO WOULD KNOW MY NAME?
teach.b: Kuchajji stays honest all the way through. In paraphrase: the others each rise above one another; who would even know my name? She doesn't fake it.
Right after her, on the same page, comes Suchajji, the skilled bride, and her skill isn't what you'd expect. No technique, no polish.

teach.h: SUCHAJJI: WHEN YOU ARE, I HAVE ALL.
teach.b: In paraphrase: when you are with me, I have everyone; you, Master, are my wealth. Within you I live at peace. By your will a throne; by your will a beggar's road.
Her skill is belonging, and she takes the throne and the road alike.

teach.h: GUNVANTI: I BOW AT THEIR FEET.
teach.b: Then, on ang 763, Guru Arjan adds Gunvanti, the virtuous bride, and her virtue is plain: whenever I see a Sikh of the Guru, I bow, again and again, at their feet. Read in order, the three poems answer the clumsy feeling.
Clumsy doesn't shut you out; Kuchajji is in the Granth, saying it out loud. And the skill isn't a performance. It's being with the One, and bowing to the people around you.

how: Guru Nanak's Kuchajji and Suchajji and Guru Arjan's Gunvanti are read and sung by Sikhs as a set, the soul-bride learning what makes her dear to the Husband.

o: where the unskilled and skilled brides speak
where Suhi's longer bride hymns begin
where the Friend comes home, in Suhi

p: the unskilled bride: my faults overflow
when you are with me, I have all
bows at the feet of the Guru's Sikhs
a throne, or a beggar's road

s: the skilled bride is dear because she's better at things than the others
her skill is belonging: when you are with me, I have everyone.
the Granth keeps a poem in the voice of a bride who says she has no skill
Kuchajji, by Guru Nanak, on ang 762.
Gunvanti's virtue is beauty and fine manners
her virtue is bowing, again and again, at the feet of the Guru's Sikhs.

games.q: a new coworker keeps making mistakes and apologizing. a teammate says she just isn't good enough for the job. what fits ang 762?
o: agree; skill is what earns someone a place on a team.
tell her to stop apologizing and fake confidence instead.
clumsy doesn't shut anyone out; help her, and bow a little yourself.
games.why: Kuchajji's honesty is kept in the Granth, Suchajji's skill is belonging, and Gunvanti's virtue is bowing to others.

practice: Count on your fingers, slowly, things you've been given that no skill of yours earned: a friend's patience, a meal, a second chance. One finger for each breath. When you run out of fingers, rest your hands open on your knees.

wordCard.voice: Ang 762. Where Guru Nanak's Kuchajji and Suchajji sit side by side: the unskilled bride and the skilled one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Kuchaji, the unskilled one; its partner poem is Suchaji, the skilled one (ang 762).

carryVoice: Skill in love: not polish, but being there, and bowing to whoever's beside you. That's fifteen thirty-eight, clumsy and counted.
